newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Commerzbank settles German tax feud.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Commerzbank settles German tax feud.

text.p: Commerzbank AG said on Monday it had settled its feud with German tax officials over a hefty back-tax bill, in a deal seen freeing up some 100 million marks ($58 million) for its 1997 accounts.
It was hit with a bill for several hundred million marks after a raid on its premises early last year.
The bank, Germany's third largest, has since been disputing the size of the repayment, which is needed to smooth out alleged anomalies in its accounts between 1984 and 1994.

Commerzbank did not reveal how much back tax it has agreed to pay but banking sources say the sum is some 100 million marks lower than the reserves Commerzbank set aside to cover the repayment. That can now be released to boost 1997 earnings.
"The main point is that this deal will not have a negative effect but rather a positive impact on us this year," a spokesman said.
Commerzbank is still dealing with a probe by prosecutors of 11 top bank officials who signed tax receipts during the 10-year period, including chief executive Martin Kohlhaussen.
The bank has repeatedly challenged the validity of this probe, which is focusing on how the bank valued overseas business and booked losses generated abroad at group level.
There has been no suggestion that managers were personally involved in evading tax.
"We still say that nobody knowingly did anything illegal during this period. This was a difference of opinion with the tax department," Commerzbank's spokesman said.
In a statement, the bank went on to say that there were minimal rules on tax conditions related to overseas business during the 1980s.

"Commerzbank remains of the opinion that there are no grounds to suspect illegal actions on tax and therefore there is absolutely no basis for speculation about changes on the supervisory board," the statement said.
The German media has been reporting that the chairman of Commerzbank's supervisory board, Walter Seipp, might be ousted as a result of the ongoing investigation.
On the basis of the agreement with finance authorities, Commerzbank should be in a position to declare some 100 million marks as extraordinary income this year.
The bank has already held out the prospect of its first dividend increase since 1994 on its results this year, amid expectations of a double-digit increase in operating profit.
Commerzbank's operating profit before risk provisions rose to 1.86 billion marks in 1996 from 1.45 billion the previous year.
